title: What To Do If You Work For a Micromanager
author: Parker Houston
summary: This article explores the psychological roots of micromanagement and provides practical strategies for employees working under controlling managers. Parker Houston examines why leaders micromanage—including fear of losing control, insecurity, perfectionism, and pressure from above—and offers seven evidence-based approaches for managing the situation. Rather than attempting to change the micromanager, Houston recommends focusing on behaviors you can control, from ensuring competence and reliability to scheduling regular check-ins and explaining your reasoning. The article acknowledges that toxic situations may warrant leaving the job entirely, emphasizing that your mental and physical health must take priority.
points: Fear of losing control, insecurity, perfectionism, and external pressure drive micromanagement behaviors that are often rooted in childhood patterns and anxiety reduction strategies. Make sure you are competent and reliable, spend time clarifying deliverables upfront, and schedule regular project updates to preempt constant checking-in. Provide your boss with options and input to satisfy their need for control, and always explain your reasoning so they understand your thought process. Do not attempt to change the micromanager, as this causes mutual frustration; instead, focus on recognizing their good qualities and adjusting your own behaviors. If you have tried multiple strategies for months and remain frustrated, it may be necessary to recognize the situation is toxic and change jobs to prioritize your wellbeing.
quotes: It's far better to focus on how you can see their good qualities and adjust to their style by focusing on your own behaviors.
Jack seemed to send a constant message, 'I want you to take full ownership of this issue….just run everything by me first.' Clint felt trapped, suffocated.
Sometimes, Clint would make a decision and Jack would undermine his leadership by stepping in and changing the decision.
If you are being micromanaged, it's often unintentional and the micromanager may not even be aware they are doing it.
